**Helping Every Child Succeed in Math: Our Move to Learning Together**

Dear Parents and Carers,

At our school, we want every single student to leave us with the math skills, confidence, and qualifications they need for a bright future. 

To make sure this happens, we are making an important change to how we teach math. Starting next term, we will stop grouping students into "high," "middle," and "low" math classes (often called "streaming" or "setting"). Instead, students will learn together in **mixed classrooms**. 

We know this is a big change, and you might have questions or worries about it. We want to explain why we are doing this and how it will help your child.

---

### Why are we making this change?

In the past, schools believed that separating children by their test scores was the best way to teach. However, years of research and our own experience have shown us that this often holds children back. 

Here is why we are moving to mixed classrooms:

#### 1. We want to remove the "ceiling" on your child’s learning
When children are put into a "lower" math group early on, it is very hard for them to move up. They often start to believe, *"I’m just not good at math."* 

In a mixed classroom, we do not decide early on what a child can or cannot achieve. Every student has the chance to reach the highest levels. We want all of our students to believe they can succeed.

#### 2. It helps students who find math difficult
When students who struggle with math sit next to classmates who understand it a bit quicker, amazing things happen. They get to hear how their classmates solve problems, which helps them learn. They also don’t feel the shame or embarrassment of being placed in the "bottom" class. 

#### 3. It helps students who are already good at math
Parents of children who do well in math often worry: *"Will my child be held back or get bored?"* 

The answer is **no**. In fact, this change will help them do even better. 
* **Deep learning, not just fast learning:** Being good at math isn't just about finishing a worksheet quickly. It is about understanding *why* the math works. 
* **Learning by teaching:** In mixed classrooms, stronger students will have the chance to explain their thinking to others. Explaining a math problem to someone else is one of the best ways to master it. It turns "good" math students into "excellent" math students.

#### 4. It prepares them for the real world
In any job, people have to work with others who have different strengths. Learning together teaches our students how to help each other, listen, and solve problems as a team. 

---

### Common Questions

**"Will the teacher still support my child if they are struggling?"**
Yes, absolutely. Teachers will still be checking on every student. If your child needs extra help, the teacher will give it to them. We will also still offer extra support outside of regular class time for students who need it.

**"How can one teacher teach students with different levels of math?"**
Our teachers are highly trained. They use math problems that have **"low floors and high ceilings."** This means the math task is simple enough for everyone to start, but has extra-challenging parts so that students who understand quickly can push themselves even further. No one will be sitting around with nothing to do.

**"Will this affect my child’s exams?"**
No. This change is designed to *improve* exam results for everyone. By keeping expectations high for all students, we are giving everyone the best possible chance to pass their exams when the time comes.

---

### We are in this together

We know that you want the absolute best for your child. So do we. We are making this change because we believe—and the evidence shows—that this is the best way to help every child succeed, no matter where they are starting from.

We welcome your feedback and would love to talk to you. If you have any questions, please feel free to contact [Name of Contact/Math Department] or come to our Parent Information Evening on [Date/Time].

Thank you for your continued support.

Warmly,

**[Principal/Headteacher Name]**
